entities.summary:
Pope Stephen V, who reigned as the bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States from September 885 until his death on 14 September 891, navigated a tumultuous period marked by the decline of Carolingian imperial authority and intensifying ecclesiastical tensions between Rome and Constantinople. His pontificate is notable for its assertive defense of papal primacy, echoing the policies of Pope Nicholas I, and for his efforts to stabilize the papacy's temporal and spiritual influence amidst political fragmentation across Western Europe. Stephen V directly engaged with the complex religious landscape of the emerging Slavic Christian states and the enduring schism with Patriarch Photius I of Constantinople.

During his six-year papacy, Stephen V took decisive actions to consolidate papal power. He crowned Guy III of Spoleto as Holy Roman Emperor in 891, a move designed to secure imperial protection for Rome while simultaneously asserting the papacy's prerogative in bestowing the imperial title. Economically, he worked to alleviate famine in Rome and successfully redeemed papal properties that had been usurped, demonstrating a practical approach to governance. Ecclesiastically, he vigorously upheld Rome's jurisdiction over the newly Christianized Bulgarians and Moravians, dispatching legates and letters to assert Latin rites and doctrines against Eastern influences, particularly in Great Moravia, where he consecrated new bishops for the Slavic church.
